description: Building AstroStress — a stress detection system for astronauts using real physiological data (WESAD dataset) with HRV analysis and personalized machine learning. Skills: Python, scikit-learn, signal processing, data visualization. Open to teammates with frontend/UI or space science interest!
summary:
AstroStress is a research prototype exploring how explainable machine learning and space-environment data analysis could support future context-aware crew health monitoring during long-duration space missions. The project investigates two complementary research areas: physiological stress detection using wearable sensor data and independent analysis of environmental conditions recorded aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
We trained and evaluated a Random Forest classifier using the WESAD dataset, containing ECG and electrodermal activity (EDA) recordings. We applied Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation to evaluate performance on participants excluded from model training. The model achieved 88.74% mean accuracy, 78.35% mean Stress F1, and a pooled ROC-AUC of 0.9436.
AstroStress also incorporates SHAP-based explainability to investigate which physiological features influence the model's predictions, alongside confidence and reliability analysis to examine how prediction accuracy varies with model confidence.
The project also analyzes real NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) environmental telemetry associated with ISS Rodent Research missions. This analysis explores recorded CO₂ concentrations, temperature, humidity, environmental trends, and data-quality characteristics such as timestamp gaps and repeated sensor readings.
AstroStress demonstrates an initial framework for interpretable physiological stress assessment and environmental monitoring.
details:
Project Details

What is AstroStress?

AstroStress is an explainable AI research prototype investigating physiological stress detection and space-environment monitoring to support the development of future crew health decision-support systems. The project brings together two research areas: stress classification using wearable physiological signals and environmental data analysis using NASA ISS telemetry.

Problem Statement

Astronauts operate in demanding environments where physiological stress can affect wellbeing, concentration, and performance during critical mission activities.

NASA already uses physiological health monitoring and environmental monitoring systems aboard the International Space Station (ISS). However, collecting sensor readings alone does not automatically provide interpretable stress predictions, confidence estimates, or actionable context for crew health decisions.

Existing research demonstrates the potential of machine learning for stress detection, but challenges remain in understanding why a model makes a prediction, how reliable that prediction is, and how environmental conditions could eventually contribute to a more complete assessment.

AstroStress addresses this research gap by investigating explainable physiological stress detection, prediction reliability, and NASA environmental telemetry analysis as complementary foundations for future context-aware crew health monitoring.

How does it work?

1. Physiological Stress Detection

Using the WESAD dataset, we extracted 19 features from ECG and EDA recordings collected from 15 participants. We compared Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost and LightGBM using Leave-One-Subject-Out cross-validation.

The selected Random Forest achieved 88.74% mean accuracy, 78.35% mean Stress F1 and 0.9436 pooled ROC-AUC.

2. Explainability and Reliability

SHAP analysis identifies the physiological features influencing the model's decisions.

We also evaluated confidence-based prediction reliability. Overall held-out accuracy was 88.65%, increasing to 94.24% on the approximately 80% of windows meeting an illustrative confidence cutoff. This demonstrates the trade-off between prediction accuracy and coverage.

3. NASA Space Environment Monitoring

We analyzed real NASA environmental telemetry associated with ISS Rodent Research missions RR-1 and RR-6, examining CO₂, temperature, humidity, weekly trends and data-quality characteristics.

4. Interactive Crew Check-in

The web application includes a mission-focused self-assessment where users select a mission scenario and enter stress, sleep, fatigue, workload, focus and wellbeing information. It provides a scenario-based crew briefing independently of the trained physiological model.

Benefits and Intended Impact

AstroStress demonstrates how explainability, confidence analysis and environmental awareness could contribute to future crew health monitoring. For long-duration missions, these capabilities could help researchers investigate earlier stress detection, more interpretable AI decisions and environmental context for health assessments.

Technology Used

  • Programming: Python, HTML, CSS, JavaScript
  • Machine Learning: Scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM
  • Explainability: SHAP
  • Data Processing: NumPy, pandas, SciPy
  • Visualization: Apache ECharts
  • Backend: Flask
  • Development and Hosting: GitHub, Vercel
  • Datasets: WESAD and NASA OSDR Environmental Data Application

Innovation

AstroStress goes beyond reporting classification accuracy by investigating three complementary capabilities:

  • Explainable AI: Understanding which physiological signals influence stress predictions.
  • Confidence-aware evaluation: Examining prediction reliability rather than treating every classification equally.
  • Environmental context: Analyzing NASA telemetry independently as a foundation for future integrated monitoring.

The physiological and environmental datasets are currently analyzed separately. Integration, astronaut-specific validation and operational crew-health triage remain future development goals.
